justification: Tasks, ServiceNow environment configs, and cheat-function grading code are all open-sourced on GitHub (WorkArena/WorkArena++), but scores are run live against a real ServiceNow enterprise instance whose demo data can drift over time; enterprise ITSM/knowledge-work workflows are less represented in generic pretraining than consumer web browsing.

The 910 tasks, environment configs, and evaluation scripts have been fully open-sourced on GitHub since the January 2024 release with no refresh since; visually-grounded web interaction (screenshots + Set-of-Marks) has moderate internet precedent, less than pure text/DOM tasks.

Task prompts are public, but grading now runs against continuously updated human-annotation snapshots (dated files from mid-2025 through late 2025) and a live-web judge, and the leaderboard keeps adding fresh model submissions through mid-2026 -- the paper's own thesis is that agents' 'illusion of progress' shows up only when re-tested live on real, currently-changing high-traffic sites; the underlying skill (mainstream consumer site navigation) is well represented in pretraining.

The 643 tasks and code are public on GitHub, but there is no fixed answer key -- correctness is judged live by a GPT-4V evaluator against the current state of 15 real, currently-live consumer websites (Amazon, Google, Booking, etc.), a task genre extremely well represented in pretraining; the task list itself has not been refreshed since the 2024 release.

Task descriptions are published on Hugging Face but grading/eval infrastructure is run by the vendor (Halluminate) and the dataset has been actively expanded and re-run (452 live sites, updated May 2025 and again by mid-2026); READ/WRITE coverage including auth, CAPTCHAs, and file downloads is less represented in pretraining than simple browsing.

Task prompts are public via the AssistantBench Hugging Face dataset and paper, but the official test-set gold answers are held out behind a leaderboard submission process typical of academic benchmarks; long-horizon, expert-level 'time-consuming assistant request' tasks requiring multi-page synthesis are a task genre with comparatively little direct internet precedent, reflected in every model scoring under 27% accuracy at release.

All 150+ tasks, the reproducible Azure-based evaluation harness, and even the scoring scripts are open-sourced on GitHub with no refresh since the September 2024 release; Windows desktop GUI control (icons, keyboard shortcuts, Office apps) has less pretraining representation than web/text tasks, evidenced by the ~20% ceiling for the best zero-shot VLM agent vs. 74.5% human performance.

The 750 tasks, 457 simulated APIs, and state-based grading code are open-sourced (ACL'24 Best Resource Paper, appworld.dev), and the official leaderboard has continued accepting new dated submissions from mid-2024 through 2026, but the fixed task set itself has not been refreshed; grading against resulting application state (not an LLM judge) is closer to code-execution testing, giving it moderate novelty versus generic text QA.

The full dataset, 2,000+ annotated tasks across 137 real (2023-era) websites, and test-set answers were released in full on Hugging Face/GitHub for the original 2023 NeurIPS paper and have not been refreshed since; general web element-selection/DOM interaction closely resembles common crawled HTML data, and this predecessor benchmark is now explicitly described as superseded by its own successor (Online-Mind2Web).

The 100+ simulated-browser micro-tasks and their programmatic reward functions have been fully open-source since 2017/2018 and unchanged since; simple synthetic UI widgets (buttons, forms, sliders) are low-novelty and, given the benchmark's age and its ubiquity as an RL/agent-training target for nearly a decade, carry real risk of direct training-data leakage despite the low intrinsic task complexity.

Modeled explicitly on Chatbot/Copilot Arena, BrowserArena scores agents via continuously arriving user-submitted tasks and step-level human (Prolific) or LLM-judge feedback on the live open web rather than any published, fixed answer key, making fresh task supply and a changing live-web environment its core anti-contamination design; open-web browsing under adversarial conditions (CAPTCHAs, pop-ups) is a moderately novel stress test even though basic browsing is common in pretraining.

The 100 tasks and project files are shared for the 2023 paper, but milestone-based success grading is implemented via bespoke scripts/critic prompts rather than a published fixed answer key; screenshot-level GUI action sequences inside complex creative/productivity software (After Effects, Premiere, MS Word) are a task genre with very little direct internet precedent, reflected in a 46% best-case success rate even with GPT-4 as both planner and actor.

The 340 cross-app, bilingual (English/Chinese) Android tasks and full evaluation pipeline are public (ICLR'25 Spotlight, GitHub), but automated success detection relies on a GPT-4o MLLM judge rather than a disclosed fixed answer key, and the task set has not been refreshed since the October 2024 release; smartphone app GUI automation has moderate representation in pretraining, lower for Chinese-language apps specifically.
